source_content.content: We conduct experiments to answer the following research questions: RQ1: Does PRAISE outperform existing baselines? RQ2: How effective is joint optimization with a shared prefix evaluator? RQ3: What is the contribution of process rewards to the overall performance of PRAISE? RQ4: Is PRAISE robust to different choices of the process-reward weight $\alpha$, and what value works best? ### 4.1 Experimental Settings #### Datasets. We train PRAISE on HotpotQA*Yang et al. ([2018](#bib.bib34 ""))* and 2WikiMultihopQA*Ho et al. ([2020](#bib.bib8 ""))*, and evaluate on NQ*Kwiatkowski et al. ([2019](#bib.bib12 ""))*, HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, Bamboogle*Press et al. ([2022](#bib.bib21 ""))*, and MuSiQue*Trivedi et al. ([2022](#bib.bib28 ""))*. #### Baselines. We compare against four categories of baselines: (1) non-agentic methods, including direct LLM answering and naive RAG*Lewis et al. ([2020](#bib.bib14 ""))*; (2) agentic search methods, including Search-o1*Li et al. ([2025](#bib.bib15 ""))*, Search-R1*Jin et al. ([2025](#bib.bib10 ""))*, and R1-Searcher*Song et al. ([2025](#bib.bib25 ""))*; (3) process-supervision methods, including StepSearch*Zheng et al. ([2025](#bib.bib38 ""))*, ReasonRAG*Zhang et al. ([2025](#bib.bib37 ""))*, and TIPS*Xie et al. ([2026](#bib.bib32 ""))*. #### Implementation Details. We use Qwen2.5-7B*Team ([2024](#bib.bib27 ""))* as the base model, verl111 as the training framework, E5*Wang et al. ([2022](#bib.bib30 ""))* as the retriever, and Wikipedia as the retrieval corpus. We report EM and F1 as the evaluation metrics. The process-reward weight $\alpha$ is set to $0.5$. *(a) Turn 0* *(b) Turn 1* *(c) Turn 2* *(d) F1 gain* *Figure 2: Step-wise analysis of the prefix evaluator under different optimization strategies. Panels (a)–(c) show the evaluator’s F1 across training steps for prefixes taken at Turn 0, Turn 1, and Turn 2, respectively. Panel (d) reports the corresponding F1 gain of joint optimization over the strongest non-joint baseline at each turn.* ### 4.2 Main Results Analysis (RQ1) Table[1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Joint optimization with PPO. ‣ 3.3 Intermediate Step Rewards and Joint Optimization ‣ 3 Prefix-Based Rollout Reuse with Intermediate Step Rewards ‣ PRAISE: Prefix-Based Rollout Reuse in Agentic Search Training") shows that PRAISE achieves the best results on all five benchmarks in both F1 and EM, consistently outperforming prior baselines from agentic search, rollout reuse, and process-supervision categories. This gives a clear positive answer to RQ1. The gains over strong agentic search baselines such as R1-Searcher are substantial, especially on HotpotQA and 2Wiki, suggesting that PRAISE is particularly effective for multi-hop reasoning tasks that require sustained evidence accumulation across search turns. PRAISE also clearly outperforms PPO baselines with repeated updates on the same rollout data, indicating that its benefit comes not simply from more reuse, but from more effective reuse of informative prefixes. In addition, PRAISE surpasses process-supervision methods such as StepSearch, ReasonRAG, and TIPS, showing that reward assignment based on adjacent prefix gains provides a stronger training signal. *Table 2: Ablation results of PRAISE on three representative benchmarks. $\Delta$ denotes the performance difference compared with the full PRAISE model.* | Method | HotpotQA | | 2Wiki | | MuSiQue | | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | | F1 | $\Delta$ | F1 | $\Delta$ | F1 | $\Delta$ | | PRAISE | 60.62 | - | 58.14 | - | 30.73 | - | | w/o joint optimization | | | | | | | | Policy model | 57.16 | -3.46 | 57.81 | -0.33 | 27.46 | -3.27 | | Frozen Qwen 7b | 57.65 | -2.97 | 57.93 | -0.21 | 27.88 | -2.85 | | Frozen Qwen 14b | 57.57 | -3.05 | 58.85 | +0.71 | 26.93 | -3.8 | | w/o process reward | 58.8 | -1.82 | 58.64 | +0.5 | 27.62 | -3.11 | | w/o prefix evaluator | 58.42 | -2.20 | 58.00 | -0.14 | 28.79 | -1.94 | *(a) 7B model on F1* *(b) 7B model on EM* *(c) 14B model on F1* *(d) 14B model on EM* *Figure 3: Effect of the process-reward weight $\alpha$ under different model sizes and evaluation metrics. None denotes the variant without prefix evaluator. The settings 0–1.0 correspond to different values of the process-reward weight $\alpha$. A larger $\alpha$ assigns a higher weight to the process reward relative to the final reward.* ### 4.3 Ablation Study on Evaluator Design and Training Strategy (RQ2) Table[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2 Main Results Analysis (RQ1) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ PRAISE: Prefix-Based Rollout Reuse in Agentic Search Training") reports ablation results on three representative benchmarks. PRAISE denotes the full model with a shared prefix evaluator, joint optimization, and intermediate process rewards. Under w/o joint optimization, we replace the shared evaluator with a separate model and consider three variants: using the policy model itself, a frozen Qwen2.5-7B, or a frozen Qwen2.5-14B as the evaluator. w/o process reward sets $\alpha\=0$, removing the contribution of intermediate rewards while keeping the rest of the framework unchanged. w/o prefix evaluator removes the prefix-evaluation module entirely and trains only on the main search rollout. Overall, the full PRAISE model performs best across benchmarks, showing that the shared and jointly optimized evaluator is an important part of the framework. When joint optimization is removed and the policy model is directly reused as the evaluator without dedicated evaluator training, RL increasingly specializes the model toward the search objective, which can weaken its more general ability to assess prefix quality. As a result, the induced process rewards become less reliable, and this variant can even perform worse than removing the evaluator altogether. Frozen evaluators, including larger models, also underperform because they do not stay aligned with the evolving search policy during training, leading to inaccurate estimates of intermediate prefix quality. By contrast, joint optimization keeps the evaluator synchronized with the current search model, enabling more faithful step-level evaluation and higher-quality process rewards. Finally, removing process rewards or removing prefix evaluation also degrades performance, confirming that both intermediate supervision and prefix-based rollout reuse are important to the effectiveness of PRAISE. ### 4.4 How Joint Optimization Shapes the Prefix Evaluator (RQ3) To understand why joint optimization helps, we analyze the prefix evaluator at different search stages during training. We compare three settings: No-train evaluator (the frozen initial reference model), Non-joint optimization (training the search policy without updating the evaluator), and Joint optimization (the full PRAISE framework). We cap the maximum number of search turns and measure the evaluator’s answer F1 at Turn 0, Turn 1, and Turn 2. To make the advantage of joint optimization more explicit, we additionally report its step-wise F1 gain relative to the stronger of the other two settings, i.e., the higher F1 between non-joint optimization and the frozen evaluator at each step. As shown in Figure[2](#S4.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Implementation Details. ‣ 4.1 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ PRAISE: Prefix-Based Rollout Reuse in Agentic Search Training"), joint optimization consistently achieves the best performance across all prefix steps, while non-joint optimization remains below it and the frozen evaluator performs worst. This shows that the evaluator itself improves during training, and that such improvement is strongest when it is optimized jointly with the search policy. ### 4.5 Effect of the Process-Reward Weight (RQ4) Figure[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.2 Main Results Analysis (RQ1) ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ PRAISE: Prefix-Based Rollout Reuse in Agentic Search Training") shows the effect of the process-reward weight $\alpha$ under different model sizes and evaluation metrics. The experiment is conducted by training on 2Wiki and evaluating on 2Wiki, using both 7B and 14B models. None denotes the variant without the entire prefix-evaluation module, and thus without process rewards. $\alpha\=0$ keeps prefix-answer training but removes process rewards. Other values of $\alpha$ correspond to different weights assigned to the process reward. The results show that removing prefix evaluation or setting $\alpha\=0$ generally leads to worse performance, confirming the importance of both prefix-based training and process rewards. For the 14B model, jointly training prefix answers without process rewards can even hurt performance, suggesting that prefix supervision alone is insufficient without reward-based guidance. In contrast, positive values of $\alpha$ consistently improve performance over the no-process-reward setting, indicating that PRAISE is reasonably robust to the choice of $\alpha$.
